newsitem.title: USA: Other carriers seen following AT&T cuts.
newsitem.headline: Other carriers seen following AT&T cuts.

text.p: AT&T Corp's reduction of 5-15 percent in basic long-distance telephone rates is expected to be followed by other long distance providers.
"Other carriers will follow through, but they haven't been as specific as AT&T in saying how or when," said Bob Wilkes, analyst with Brown Brothers Harriman.
"Typically, the others do follow, although not in lock step" said Frank Governali, telecommunications analyst with CS First Boston Corp.

The reductions stem from about $1.7 billion in annual savings the long distance companies will realize from Federal Communications Commission-ordered cuts in the access charges they pay to Baby Bell companies.
"This is what they committed to the FCC they would do," Governali said.
The access charge reductions take effect Tuesday.
Estimates for the AT&T share of the savings pie hover between $900 million and $930 million, given that it controls more than half the long distance market, analysts said.
AT&T was the only one of the major long distance carriers to commit in writing to the FCC that it would pass on all of its share of the rate reductions savings.
Sprint Corp spokeswoman Robin Pence said, "We haven't determined specifically what we're going to do."
Sprint had not determined its share of the savings from the access charge cuts, Pence said. "If our costs go down, we will pass on the savings to our customers as we have in the past."
Calls to MCI Communications Corp for details of how it will handle the access reductions were not immediately returned.
AT&T said it expects its competitors to follow suit.

"The supposition is that all the savings will be flowed through to customers," said AT&T spokesman Jim McGann. "In a competitive environment like this, no one can really afford to hang onto a cost savings and not pass it on to customers."

McGann said most of the savings will be realized by basic rate customers. Members of other rate plans probably will see some benefit, he said, but he would not elaborate. "Those details will be part of marketing promotions that we're not revealing for now."
The company declined to say how soon the promotions would go into effect.

Hours after AT&T revealed Monday its plan to cut rates for daytime and evening calls by five percent and night and weekend calls by 15 percent, Bell Atlantic Corp said it filed a complaint with the FCC alleging AT&T was pocketing some of the savings.
Bell spokeswoman Shannon Fioravanti said AT&T had hedged on its pledge in recent weeks and said Bell Atlantic is not convinced AT&T is passing on all the savings.

"If they live up to that promise, they will be living up to what they promised to the FCC on May 7, but we're suspicious, and we think AT&T customers should be suspicious, particularly basic rate payers," Fioravanti said.
AT&T would not specifically respond to the allegation, but said it was not pocketing any savings.
"We are passing the savings on, period," AT&T spokesman Mark Siegel said.
